stumbles.quote: remex's hash cells hold 70% while scanning 34%
stumbles.why: remex is never explained, and the 'hash cells' (what hash, e.g. LSH or sign bits) are undefined. The first sentence implies hash cells are a generic method, but here they belong to remex.
e-means is never defined. A k-means engineer can't tell how it differs from Lloyd's, and the arXiv citation is the only pointer.
Refers to earlier work by an unnamed 'our' (Oskar and the author) that the text never describes.

stumbles.quote: I had assumed that e-means would mainly speed up training, and that coding vectors as offsets would be the win while index cells would be a side note; it came out the other way.
stumbles.why: It is unclear what 'the other way' reverses. The text then says the choice of algorithm affects only training time, which seems to contradict the first assumption's reversal.
The quantization scheme is not explained, and 'adding a second bit per dimension' is unclear against it. The baseline for recall 0.840 vs 0.891 is also unstated.

stumbles.quote: the centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector
stumbles.why: The figure is unexplained. 4,096 centroids × the dimensions × 4 bytes divided by 100,000 vectors depends on a dimension count never given, and it isn't compared with the actual cost of a second bit.

stumbles.quote: matches the error of 25 iterations of Lloyd's k-means in 1 to 3 passes
stumbles.why: 'Passes' is undefined for e-means, and 'error' is not defined (e.g. quantization MSE). The speedup range of 1.6 to 10.2 times is not tied to those pass counts.
This is recall of what, and in what setup? It is not obviously the same measure as the '90% of true neighbours' capture, and the offset-coded result is never set against the index-cell result.

point: Using e-means centroids as index cells captures 90% of true neighbours while scanning only 0.56% of 100k vectors (versus 70% at 34% for remex's hash cells), and e-means mainly cuts training time compared with Lloyd's k-means.
